slides.title: Understanding Concurrency vs Parallelism & the GIL
slides.prompt: Concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once (task switching), while parallelism is about doing lots of things at once (simultaneous execution). Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) limits CPython execution to a single native thread at a time.
slides.codeSnippet:
import sys
import threading

# Checking thread GIL switch interval
print(f"GIL switch interval: {sys.getswitchinterval()} seconds")

# Concurrency allows overlapping task execution
# Parallelism requires multiple CPU cores

slides.title: Bypassing GIL Constraints
slides.prompt: What is the primary method to achieve true CPU-bound parallelism in Python on multi-core hardware?
options: Using multiprocessing to launch separate OS processes with independent GILs
Increasing the number of standard threads
slides.correctAnswer: Using multiprocessing to launch separate OS processes with independent GILs

slides.title: GIL Behavior During I/O
slides.prompt: What happens to the GIL when a Python thread performs a blocking I/O operation (like downloading a web page)?
options: The thread releases the GIL, allowing other threads to execute Python code
The GIL locks all other OS threads until I/O completes
The Python interpreter terminates with a DeadlockError
The GIL creates a duplicate interpreter instance automatically
slides.correctAnswer: The thread releases the GIL, allowing other threads to execute Python code
